q: On the straight-line path (1-s)H0 + s H1 with projector Hamiltonians, our final fidelity plateaus at ~0.997-0.999 rather than approaching 1 as T grows (experiment D actually gets slightly WORSE from T=10 F=0.998 to T=200 F=0.9972). What is the residual? Is it discretization error from s_k = k/T never exactly reaching s=1, diabatic phase pickup within the 2D invariant subspace, or something else, and does a boundary-vanishing schedule s(u)=sin^2(pi u/2) eliminate the plateau?
basis: The paper predicts high fidelity is achievable but doesn't discuss the specific saturating value. Our numerics show a distribution-dependent floor that is present at every T we tried and even grows slightly with T for the sharpest distribution -- a numerical signature that deserves attention.
next_steps: (a) Rerun with a smoothed schedule s(u)=sin^2(pi u/2) and with the paper's suggested Zeno-effect discretization (Appendix); (b) sweep t_tot at fixed T=200 to isolate discretization vs adiabatic error; (c) analytically diagonalize the 2x2 block and derive the closed-form residual; (d) check whether the residual is exactly the transition amplitude Landau-Zener predicts for the near-avoided-crossing at s=1/2.

q: The projector Hamiltonian H1 = I - |psi><psi| is generally NOT row-sparse in the computational basis when |psi> is a superposition, yet the paper's Sparse Hamiltonian Lemma requires row-sparse row-computable H. What is the actual sparse surrogate H_check used to simulate this specific H1 for a generic samplable p, and does its spectral gap match the dense-projector gap that governs our observed scaling?
basis: Our replication used the dense H1 directly (matrix-exponentiate a 256x256 rank-1 perturbation of identity). A hardware-honest replication needs the sparse surrogate to make the wall-time claim; the paper cites Kitaev phase estimation as the tool but the explicit construction and its own gap behavior is not spelled out.
next_steps: (a) Build H_check as a projector via phase-estimation on the Q-sampling circuit U_p (|0..0> -> |psi>): H_check = U_p (I - |0..0><0..0|) U_p^dagger; verify it is 3-local + sparse; (b) simulate H(s) = (1-s)H0 + s H_check at n=4..10 qubits and compare gaps to the dense form; (c) time-cost comparison at n=8 between the dense projector and the sparse phase-estimation-based projector; (d) reproduce for the paper's DLPc and QR examples (Sec 2.4-2.5) where the states are known analytically.

q: We used dense H0 = I - |+^n><+^n|; the physically realistic choice is the 1-local transverse-field H0 = sum_i (I - X_i)/2 (Grover / Farhi-style), which also has |+^n> as unique ground state but is sparse. Does the min-gap of (1-s)H0_local + s H1_sparse scale polynomially or exponentially in n for the paper's SZK-derived target states, and does the observed empirical scaling change from 1/gap^2 to 1/gap^3?
basis: The all-dense construction sidesteps the physical scaling question. This is the difference between an operationally-nice framework paper and an actually-implementable algorithm on near-term hardware; our small-n numerics can address it directly.
next_steps: (a) Reimplement H0 as the sum-of-transverse-field local operator; verify |+^n> ground state remains; (b) sweep n from 4 to 14, plotting log(gap_min) vs n for uniform, Bernoulli, and cospan targets; (c) fit polynomial vs exponential decay; (d) compare with the Farhi-Goldstone-Gutmann adiabatic-vs-QAA scaling literature (this is essentially the AQC-vs-Grover question in a state-generation guise).

q: Our T-vs-gap scan (t_needed = 5, 5, 5, 10, 20, 40 as gap_min drops 1.0 -> 0.96 -> 0.84 -> 0.66 -> 0.41 -> 0.27) is closer to the smoothed-schedule bound t ~ 1/gap^2 than the naive linear-schedule bound t ~ 1/gap^3. Which regime governs the paper's construction, and does the 1/gap^2 empirical fit extend to n >= 15 where higher-order corrections should kick in?
basis: The paper cites both O(1/gap^2) and O(1/gap^3) regimes without committing. The exact exponent is what makes adiabatic state generation polynomial or superpolynomial for realistic instances; our data show the friendlier scaling for n=8 but this needs testing at larger n.
next_steps: (a) Extend the C2 scan to n=12, 14, 16 (Hilbert space up to 65k -- still feasible in numpy with 2D-subspace trick); (b) fit t_needed = A/gap^alpha and estimate alpha with confidence intervals; (c) try three schedules (linear s=u; Jansen-Ruskai-Seiler s(u) with vanishing 1st derivative at endpoints; Wan-Kim double-vanishing) and see which alpha they select; (d) check whether alpha depends on distribution shape (product vs coset vs random support).

q: Claim 1 verifies <psi_0|psi_1> = F(p_0, p_1) exactly, and the paper argues this makes the Hadamard-test SZK decider work. But the end-to-end concrete cost of the SZK-decision procedure -- adiabatic evolution twice (once per circuit C_i) at cost O(1/Delta_min^k), plus O(log(1/delta)) Hadamard repetitions to distinguish 1+sqrt(1-alpha^2)/2 vs 1-beta/2 -- is never estimated numerically in the paper. What is that end-to-end wall-cost as a function of (n, alpha, beta, Delta_min), and does it actually beat the best classical SD algorithm at the small instance sizes we can simulate?
basis: SZK subset BQP is a structural containment, not a benchmarked algorithm. Our C3 identity check is one piece; the full pipeline has never been end-to-end costed even at the toy scale.
next_steps: (a) Instrument the full SZK-decider: build two toy SD instances (yes vs no) at n=6..10 bits with alpha=3/4, beta=1/4; (b) prepare 1/sqrt(2)(|0>|psi_0>+|1>|psi_1>) coherently via two parallel adiabatic evolutions; (c) run the Hadamard test with O(log(1/delta)) reps and measure decision accuracy vs adiabatic-evolution time budget; (d) compare against classical SD via sampling from C_0 and C_1 and estimating the L1 distance -- which crossover point does BQP actually win, and does it exist in the small-n regime?
